name: Diego Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a seven-person agency that mostly does packaging and labels for food and drink brands: small breweries, an olive oil company, a hot sauce guy who changes his mind every week. I get in around nine, check what the printer flagged overnight, then spend most of the day in Illustrator building label artwork and checking it against die lines, which are the cutting shapes for the box or label. The part I love is holding a printed sample in my hand. The part that wears me out is the tenth round of "can the logo be bigger".

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with most, and how do you use your evenings?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marta owns the agency and still does the client calls; I sit next to Sam, who's a junior and does a lot of the mockups. My girlfriend Ana is a physiotherapist, so her days are long too, and most evenings we just cook and watch something. Money-wise I'm lucky: I've got about ten months saved, and my sister and I rent out the small flat our grandmother left us. I use AI now and then, mostly for mood boards and cutting out backgrounds, but I don't build my day around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds a lot like right now, honestly. The tools get a bit better every few months and then everyone goes back to arguing about fonts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a handy tool, it saves me twenty minutes on a mockup, and clients still want a person who gets their brand. At the pub with other designers I'd probably joke that the robots took the boring bits and left us the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. My job stays my job, my pay keeps going up a little each year, and the flat keeps paying its share. The only thing that bugs me is that the routine stuff AI does take, like resizing a label for six bottle sizes, is exactly the work my junior colleague Sam does. His role might get thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much nothing dramatic. I'd keep doing the packaging work, ask Marta in my spring review for a bit more on the print-production side, and maybe learn the new background and resizing tools properly instead of half-learning them. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into savings like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's a world where my plan for the next few years still works, and that's a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Sam. What would that look like for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam spends maybe half his week on resizing and versioning, so if software does that in a click, Marta might not need a full-time junior. I'd tell Sam to get good at press checks and talking to printers, because that's the bit no tool does. I'd hate to see him let go over something that small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent in our area keeps going up, and Ana and I want to buy something in the next three years. That's the real pressure, AI or no AI. But with the savings and the flat income, I think we can do it, so it's a worry I can actually plan around.

say: AI is a **handy tool** that saves me twenty minutes on a mockup, nothing more.
Clients still want a **person who gets** their brand and their shelf.
think: My **job and pay** stay on track, and the inherited flat keeps paying its share.
The **resizing work** AI takes is mostly what Sam the junior does, so his role thins.
do: Ask Marta for more **print-production work** at the spring review.
Learn the **resizing tools** properly instead of half-learning them.
Keep saving a **few hundred a month** towards buying a home with Ana.
feel: **Calm**, because his plan for the next few years still holds.
A small **worry for Sam**, whose junior tasks are the ones that disappear.
S0.quote: The routine stuff AI does take, like resizing a label for six bottle sizes, is exactly the work my junior colleague Sam does.
fieldNote: His **security** rests on savings, an inherited flat and a steady agency, and he knows it.
He thinks about the **junior's job** before his own, which says a lot about him.
His real pressure is **buying a home** with Ana, not technology.

steps.text: Ask Marta for more print-production work at the spring review
Learn the label resizing and background tools properly
Keep saving a few hundred a month for a home deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one I can actually see happening. Half of what our clients pay us for is planning and writing and checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say design is changing and the people who know print and packaging will be fine, because a label still has to fit a real bottle. Online I'd probably share a few of the good AI label tests and the funny bad ones, to show I'm keeping up without panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the agency shrinks. If clients can get first drafts of a label from software, Marta won't hire again when someone leaves, and the fees for concepts go down. I'm about average at the job, not a star, so I could be the one asked to go part-time, or just not get the raises I was counting on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd sit down with Marta and ask straight out what she sees for next year. I'd learn the AI tools the clients are using, so I'm the one fixing their drafts rather than competing with them. I'd also put the flat income straight into savings instead of spending it, and I'd start a short course in print production and colour management at the college in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but not scared. I've got a cushion and there are other agencies in town, so it's more like a knot in my stomach than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move the flat income into savings. What would you stop spending on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd skip the big summer trip and do a week at Ana's parents' place instead, and I'd hold off on the new laptop I've been eyeing. It's not a hardship. It's just that if my pay drops, I want the house plan to survive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why print production and colour, rather than more AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the press check is where a real person standing next to a real machine still matters. I've seen a whole run of olive oil labels come out the wrong green, and it took a human with a printed swatch to catch it. If the screen part of my job gets eaten, I want to own the part that happens on paper.

I'd share **AI label tests**, good and bad, to show I'm keeping up calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before Ana and I would even have bought a place. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd try to sound sensible: something like, this is huge, nobody knows how it lands, and we all need to look after each other. I wouldn't post much, though. I'd feel a bit like a fraud saying anything confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is gone by 2028. Almost everything I do is on a screen, and if a machine can do any thinking work as well as me for less, Marta's clients just won't pay for me. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me much, because only a small slice of my week is hands-on, like press checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the house hunt and keep renting, because I wouldn't want a mortgage on an income that might vanish. I'd move every spare euro into savings and keep the flat rented, since that rent might end up being our steadiest money. I'd look for work that has a physical side, maybe at a print house or a packaging factory, where I'd be on the floor with the machines for those three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I keep thinking about the gap between 2028 and 2031: three years where my hands still count, and then that goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana the night you decided to stop the house hunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Ana that her job looks safer than mine, because patients need hands on their backs and the robots are years away. I'd say we should live on her pay and the flat rent, and treat mine as extra while it lasts. That would hurt my pride, but it's the sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for factory or print-house work. Is that realistic for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a step down in pay, maybe a third less, and I've never run a press. But there are a few print houses within a short bus ride, and I know the managers from press checks. With ten months saved I could afford to take the pay cut and learn.

He'd stay **quiet online** because sounding confident would feel fake.
think: His **screen-based job** is likely gone by 2028.
The robots' **three-year lag** barely helps, because only press checks are hands-on.

Move every **spare euro** into savings and keep the flat rented.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels different. Not good, but different. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if people start now, and I'd probably bring it up at the agency's Friday lunch. I'd want Marta and the others to talk about it instead of pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my design job still ends around 2031, but five years lets me move before the cliff instead of falling off it. I could get into print and packaging production properly and have real experience by the time AGI lands. And then I'd have until about 2034 before robots catch up on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the print-production course and ask Marta if I can run all our press checks. By year two I'd try to move to a print house full time, while the pay gap is smaller. We'd still buy a flat, but a smaller one, with a mortgage we could carry on Ana's salary alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a bit of hope in it. There's a plan here, and plans calm me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a smaller flat. What changes from your original plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wanted two bedrooms near the park so one could be my studio. Now it'd be one bedroom further out, and the mortgage would be sized to what Ana earns. My income and the rent from my grandmother's flat would go into paying it down faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd be the one asked to go. Do you still think that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, but here I'd go on my own timing. That's the whole difference with five years. I'd rather leave Marta's agency with a skill in my hands than be the last designer let go there in 2031.

steps.text: Ask Marta to let him run every press check this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade. By then I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole second career's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to change course if governments and companies are honest about it. I'd tell younger designers not to drop out, but to learn something with a physical side alongside the screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it still ends the same way for designers. But ten years is long enough that I could build something, maybe a small business making packaging prototypes, the cut-and-fold samples brands need before a print run. The robots wouldn't catch that until around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep my job and keep saving, and buy a home with Ana as we planned. In the next couple of years I'd start making prototypes on the side, using a cutting table at the print house near us on weekends. If it grew, I'd go part-time at the agency by about 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thoughtful more than scared. It's still a worry, but it's the kind I can work on in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would that side business cost to start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent sample cutting table is a few thousand euros, and I wouldn't buy one at first. I'd rent time on one and use maybe two months of my savings at most. If it didn't work in two years, I'd stop and still be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI in your work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than now, yes. Once it's clearly better, I'd use it for the drawing and keep my hands for the samples. I'm not the first to try new things, but I'm not stubborn either.

S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I could build something, maybe a small business making packaging prototypes, the cut-and-fold samples brands need before a print run.
fieldNote: He still expects his **design income to go**, which keeps him anxious, not uneasy.

steps.text: Rent weekend time on a print-house cutting table for prototypes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. It's not the job itself, it's that it lands before Ana and I have a home and before I've got any hands-on skill to fall back on. What would help is cheap evening training in print and production, and some kind of pay top-up for people who take a step down to learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what clients will want. Our hot sauce customer doesn't want a machine telling him his label is fine. That customer wants someone to argue with. Whether he'll still pay for that argument, I honestly don't know.

headlineQuote: Our hot sauce customer doesn't want a machine telling him his label is fine. That customer wants someone to argue with.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old packaging designer** at a seven-person agency, about average at the job and well paid.
His **cushion** is ten months of savings plus rent from a flat he co-owns with his sister.
He worries about **Sam the junior** in the calm picture and about his own job once change speeds up.
His answer to every faster scenario is to move toward **print production**, the hands-on side of packaging.
Buying a **home with Ana** shapes every plan, and he'd size the mortgage to her safer salary.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands before he has a home or any hands-on skill to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap evening training** in print and production work.
A **pay top-up** for people who step down to learn a trade.
